question_html: Under section 2(35) of the Companies Act, 2013, how is the term 'dividend' defined, and what does it represent in substance?

options.A: Section 2(35) simply states that 'dividend' includes any interim dividend; in substance, dividend is a distribution of a portion of a company's profits (and, where permitted, free reserves) to its members, representing their return on the investment/capital they hold in the company
options.B: Section 2(35) defines 'dividend' as a fixed, guaranteed annual payment that every company must make to its equity shareholders, irrespective of whether the company has earned any profits in that year
options.C: Section 2(35) defines 'dividend' exclusively as the final dividend declared at the Annual General Meeting, expressly excluding any interim dividend from the scope of the term
options.D: Section 2(35) defines 'dividend' as a distribution made necessarily out of a company's capital, rather than out of its profits or free reserves

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Section 2(35) simply states that 'dividend' includes any interim dividend; in substance, dividend is a distribution of a portion of a company's profits (and, where permitted, free reserves) to its members, representing their return on the investment/capital they hold in the company

Section 2(35) is an inclusive definition stating that 'dividend' includes any interim dividend. In substance, dividend is the shareholders' return on their investment/capital - a distribution of a portion of profits (and, where permitted, free reserves) that has been earned and allocated as payable to members whenever declared.

question_html: The company in general meeting may declare dividends, but can the shareholders declare a dividend at a rate higher than that recommended by the Board of Directors?

options.A: Yes - the shareholders in general meeting have unrestricted power to declare a dividend at any rate they choose, even where it exceeds the rate recommended by the Board of Directors
options.B: No - although the power to declare a dividend vests with the shareholders in general meeting, under no circumstances can they declare a dividend exceeding the amount recommended by the Board of Directors (Clause 80 of Table F to Schedule I); the members may, however, declare it at the rate recommended or at a lower rate
options.C: No - shareholders have no power at all to declare dividend; the power to both recommend and declare dividend rests exclusively with the Board of Directors under all circumstances
options.D: Yes, but only where a special resolution (rather than an ordinary resolution) is passed sanctioning a rate higher than that recommended by the Board of Directors

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - although the power to declare a dividend vests with the shareholders in general meeting, under no circumstances can they declare a dividend exceeding the amount recommended by the Board of Directors (Clause 80 of Table F to Schedule I); the members may, however, declare it at the rate recommended or at a lower rate

question_html: At what point does dividend become a legally enforceable liability of the company towards its shareholders?

options.A: Dividend becomes a liability of the company the moment the Board of Directors merely recommends it in the Board's Report, even before the shareholders have approved it at a general meeting
options.B: Dividend becomes a liability of the company automatically at the end of every financial year in which the company has earned a profit, regardless of any recommendation or declaration
options.C: Dividend is not a liability of the company unless and until it is declared by the shareholders at a validly constituted general meeting, by passing an ordinary resolution (based on the Board's recommendation)
options.D: Dividend never becomes a liability of the company at any stage, even after declaration by the shareholders at a validly constituted general meeting

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Dividend is not a liability of the company unless and until it is declared by the shareholders at a validly constituted general meeting, by passing an ordinary resolution (based on the Board's recommendation)

Dividend is not a liability unless it is declared by the shareholders at a validly constituted general meeting (by passing an ordinary resolution, at the rate recommended by the Board or a lower rate) - a mere Board recommendation, without shareholder approval, does not by itself create an enforceable liability.

question_html: Who has the power to declare an interim dividend, and during what period may it be declared?

options.A: Only the shareholders in general meeting (and never the Board of Directors) may declare an interim dividend, at any time after the accounts for the financial year have been finally adopted
options.B: The Board of Directors may declare an interim dividend only after the accounts for the financial year have been finally adopted by the shareholders at the AGM, never before such adoption
options.C: Interim dividend may be declared only once every three years, coinciding with the rotation of the company's statutory auditor
options.D: The Board of Directors may declare an interim dividend, at any time during the period from closure of the financial year till the holding of the Annual General Meeting - it is declared out of profits before the final adoption of accounts by the shareholders, and is therefore said to be declared and paid between two AGMs

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The Board of Directors may declare an interim dividend, at any time during the period from closure of the financial year till the holding of the Annual General Meeting - it is declared out of profits before the final adoption of accounts by the shareholders, and is therefore said to be declared and paid between two AGMs

Sections 123(3) and 123(4) contain the provisions on interim dividend. The Board of Directors may declare it at any time during the period from closure of the financial year till the holding of the AGM - the declaration is made out of profits before the final adoption of accounts by the shareholders, so interim dividend is said to be declared and paid between two AGMs.

question_html: What are the permitted sources out of which the Board of Directors may declare an interim dividend?

options.A: Surplus in the profit and loss account; or profits of the financial year in which such dividend is sought to be declared; or profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend
options.B: Interim dividend may be declared exclusively out of the company's share capital account, since profits (whether of the current or a previous year) cannot be used as a source for interim dividend under any circumstances
options.C: Interim dividend may be declared exclusively out of unrealised or notional gains arising from revaluation of the company's fixed assets, this being the sole permitted source under section 123(3)
options.D: Interim dividend may be declared only out of profits of financial years prior to the immediately preceding three years, and never out of the surplus in the profit and loss account or the profits of the current financial year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Surplus in the profit and loss account; or profits of the financial year in which such dividend is sought to be declared; or profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend

Section 123(3) permits interim dividend to be sourced from: surplus in the profit and loss account; or profits of the financial year in which such dividend is sought to be declared; or profits generated in the financial year till the quarter preceding the date of declaration of the interim dividend.

question_html: If a company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration of interim dividend, at what maximum rate may the Board declare such interim dividend?

options.A: Such interim dividend shall not be declared at all in any circumstance, once the company has incurred any loss up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration, regardless of the company's dividend history
options.B: Such interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the average (rate of) dividend declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years
options.C: Such interim dividend may be declared at any rate the Board considers fit, since the proviso to section 123(3) applies only to final dividend and has no application to interim dividend at all
options.D: Such interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the HIGHEST (rather than the average) rate of dividend declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Such interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the average (rate of) dividend declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years

The proviso to section 123(3) provides that where a company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration of interim dividend, such interim dividend shall not be declared at a rate higher than the AVERAGE rate of dividend declared by the company during the immediately preceding three financial years - e.g., if the company declared dividend at 16% during each of the preceding three years, it may declare interim dividend at a rate not higher than 16% despite the current-year loss.

question_html: When is a dividend referred to as 'final dividend', and by whom is it declared?

options.A: 'Final dividend' refers to a dividend declared by the Board of Directors alone, without any requirement of shareholder approval at the Annual General Meeting or otherwise
options.B: 'Final dividend' refers to a dividend that must necessarily be declared before the preparation of the financial statements for the relevant financial year, unlike interim dividend which is declared only after such preparation
options.C: When the dividend is declared at the Annual General Meeting of the company, it is known as 'final dividend' - it is declared by the shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year, on the recommendation of the Board of Directors, and is approved after preparation of the financial statements
options.D: 'Final dividend' refers to a dividend that a company is statutorily prohibited from declaring more than once, this being the meaning of the term 'final' in this context

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) When the dividend is declared at the Annual General Meeting of the company, it is known as 'final dividend' - it is declared by the shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year, on the recommendation of the Board of Directors, and is approved after preparation of the financial statements

When dividend is declared at the Annual General Meeting of the company, it is known as 'final dividend'. It is declared by the shareholders at the AGM, on the recommendation of the Board of Directors, after the close of the financial year and after preparation of the financial statements for the year - unlike interim dividend, which is declared by the Board before such preparation, between two AGMs.

question_html: What is the key distinction between interim dividend and final dividend in terms of the time of declaration relative to preparation of financial statements, and can the rate recommended by the Board for final dividend be increased by the members?

options.A: Interim dividend is always declared after finalisation of the accounts for the year, whereas final dividend is always declared before such finalisation - i.e., the reverse of the correct sequence, and the members are free to increase the Board's recommended rate for final dividend
options.B: There is no distinction at all between interim and final dividend in terms of timing relative to preparation of financial statements; both are, by definition, declared simultaneously at the AGM
options.C: Interim dividend can only be declared by the shareholders at a general meeting, never by the Board of Directors, whereas final dividend can only be declared by the Board of Directors, never by the shareholders
options.D: Interim dividend is declared and paid during an accounting year, i.e., before the finalisation of accounts for the year, whereas final dividend is the dividend recommended by the Board of Directors and approved by shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year (i.e., after preparation of financial statements); in either case, the rate recommended by the Board cannot be increased by the members

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Interim dividend is declared and paid during an accounting year, i.e., before the finalisation of accounts for the year, whereas final dividend is the dividend recommended by the Board of Directors and approved by shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year (i.e., after preparation of financial statements); in either case, the rate recommended by the Board cannot be increased by the members

Interim dividend is declared and paid during an accounting year, before finalisation of accounts, by the Board of Directors; final dividend is the dividend recommended by the Board and approved by shareholders at the AGM, after the close of the financial year (after preparation of financial statements). In both cases, the rate recommended by the Board cannot be increased by the members - they may only approve it or a lower rate.

options.A: Yes - all provisions which are applicable to the payment of dividend (e.g., deposit in a separate scheduled bank account within 5 days of declaration, payment to the registered shareholder, mode of payment, the 30-day payment timeline, and the punishment provisions) shall also apply in case of interim dividend
options.B: No - interim dividend is entirely exempt from all provisions applicable to the payment of dividend, including the requirement of depositing the amount in a separate scheduled bank account within 5 days of declaration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - all provisions which are applicable to the payment of dividend (e.g., deposit in a separate scheduled bank account within 5 days of declaration, payment to the registered shareholder, mode of payment, the 30-day payment timeline, and the punishment provisions) shall also apply in case of interim dividend

question_html: Under section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013, what dividend-related assurance do shareholders holding preference shares enjoy?

options.A: Shareholders holding preference shares are assured of an equal (not preferential) dividend rate as equity shareholders, with no priority in payment over equity shareholders
options.B: Shareholders holding preference shares are assured of a preferential dividend at a fixed rate during the life of the company
options.C: Shareholders holding preference shares are assured of a dividend at a fixed rate only for the first five years after allotment, after which they lose all preferential dividend rights entirely
options.D: Shareholders holding preference shares are guaranteed dividend payment every single year without exception, even where the company has insufficient profits, unlike any other class of shareholder

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Shareholders holding preference shares are assured of a preferential dividend at a fixed rate during the life of the company

According to section 43, shareholders holding preference shares are assured of a preferential dividend at a fixed rate during the life of the company - though, as clarified elsewhere, this assurance of a fixed rate does not by itself guarantee payment every year where profits are insufficient (unless the shares are cumulative in nature).

question_html: What happens to unpaid dividend on 'cumulative preference shares' in a year of insufficient profits, and can dividend be paid to equity shareholders while such arrears remain unpaid?

options.A: A cumulative preference share is one where any unpaid dividend for a year of insufficient profits lapses permanently at the end of that year, exactly as with a non-cumulative preference share, with no right to arrears in future years
options.B: A cumulative preference share entitles the holder to arrears of unpaid dividend, but equity shareholders may nonetheless be paid dividend in the meantime, even while such arrears on cumulative preference shares remain unpaid
options.C: A cumulative preference share is one in respect of which dividend gets accumulated, and any arrears of such dividend arising due to insufficiency of profits during the current year is payable from the profits earned in later years; until and unless dividend on cumulative preference shares is paid in full (including arrears, if any), NO dividend is payable on equity shares
options.D: A cumulative preference share converts automatically into an equity share at the end of any year in which dividend on it remains unpaid due to insufficiency of profits

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) A cumulative preference share is one in respect of which dividend gets accumulated, and any arrears of such dividend arising due to insufficiency of profits during the current year is payable from the profits earned in later years; until and unless dividend on cumulative preference shares is paid in full (including arrears, if any), NO dividend is payable on equity shares

A cumulative preference share accumulates unpaid dividend, payable out of later years' profits - and until dividend on cumulative preference shares (including all arrears) is paid in full, no dividend can be paid on equity shares, since equity shareholders rank behind preference shareholders in the priority of payment.

question_html: What is the consequence for a holder of 'non-cumulative preference shares' where the company declares no dividend in a particular year due to insufficiency of profits?

options.A: The holder of a non-cumulative preference share is entitled to receive the unpaid dividend in a subsequent year of profit, exactly as a holder of a cumulative preference share would be, since both classes carry an identical right to arrears
options.B: The holder of a non-cumulative preference share automatically becomes entitled to voting rights on every resolution at every general meeting the moment dividend is not paid in any year, regardless of the ordinary restrictions on preference shareholders' voting rights
options.C: The holder of a non-cumulative preference share is deemed, by operation of law, to have converted his holding into equity shares the moment dividend is not paid in any particular year
options.D: A non-cumulative preference share is one where dividend is payable only in a year of profit; there is no accumulation of profit as with cumulative preference shares, and if no dividend is declared in a year for any reason, the right to receive dividend for that year lapses - the holder is not entitled to be paid arrears of dividend out of future years' profits

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A non-cumulative preference share is one where dividend is payable only in a year of profit; there is no accumulation of profit as with cumulative preference shares, and if no dividend is declared in a year for any reason, the right to receive dividend for that year lapses - the holder is not entitled to be paid arrears of dividend out of future years' profits

For a non-cumulative preference share, dividend is payable only in a year of profit - there is no accumulation as with cumulative preference shares. If no dividend is declared for a year (for any reason), the right to receive dividend for that specific year simply lapses, and the holder cannot claim it out of future years' profits.

question_html: How does the dividend entitlement of equity shareholders differ from that of preference shareholders?

options.A: Equity shares are shares that are not preference shares; they do not enjoy any preferential rights in the matter of payment of dividend or repayment of capital, and the rate of dividend on equity shares depends upon the company's dividend policy and the availability of profits after satisfying the rights of preference shareholders
options.B: Equity shareholders enjoy the same preferential right to a fixed-rate dividend as preference shareholders under section 43, ranking equally (not after) preference shareholders in the priority of payment
options.C: Equity shareholders are entitled to a dividend at a fixed, statutorily prescribed rate every year, which does not vary depending on the company's dividend policy or the availability of profits
options.D: Equity shareholders are entitled to be paid dividend BEFORE preference shareholders in every case, this priority being the defining distinguishing feature of an equity share under the Companies Act, 2013

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Equity shares are shares that are not preference shares; they do not enjoy any preferential rights in the matter of payment of dividend or repayment of capital, and the rate of dividend on equity shares depends upon the company's dividend policy and the availability of profits after satisfying the rights of preference shareholders

Equity shares do not carry any preferential right to dividend or repayment of capital - unlike preference shares. The rate of dividend on equity shares is recommended by the Board of Directors, may vary from year to year, and depends upon the company's dividend policy and the availability of profits after first satisfying the rights of preference shareholders.

question_html: Is the rate of dividend on equity shares fixed permanently at the time of issue of the shares, or can it change from year to year?

options.A: The rate of dividend on equity shares is fixed permanently at the time of issue of the shares, in the same manner as the fixed rate assured to preference shareholders under section 43, and cannot thereafter vary from year to year
options.B: The rate of dividend on equity shares is recommended by the Board of Directors and may vary from year to year, depending upon the dividend policy and the availability of profits after satisfying the rights of preference shareholders - it is not fixed permanently at the time of issue, unlike the fixed rate assured to preference shareholders under section 43
options.C: The rate of dividend on equity shares is determined exclusively by the Registrar of Companies at the time of incorporation, and neither the Board of Directors nor the shareholders have any role in recommending or varying it thereafter
options.D: The rate of dividend on equity shares must, by law, remain identical every year to the rate declared in the company's very first year of operations, regardless of subsequent profitability

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The rate of dividend on equity shares is recommended by the Board of Directors and may vary from year to year, depending upon the dividend policy and the availability of profits after satisfying the rights of preference shareholders - it is not fixed permanently at the time of issue, unlike the fixed rate assured to preference shareholders under section 43

Unlike preference shares (which carry a fixed dividend rate under section 43), the rate of dividend on equity shares is recommended afresh each year by the Board of Directors and may vary from year to year, depending on the company's dividend policy and the profits available after satisfying preference shareholders' rights.

question_html: Into which two broad categories are shares classified for the purpose of determining the manner of payment of dividend?

options.A: Shares are classified into 'bonus shares' and 'rights shares' for the purpose of determining the manner of payment of dividend, a classification based on the mode of issue rather than dividend entitlement
options.B: Shares are classified into 'listed shares' and 'unlisted shares' for the purpose of determining the manner of payment of dividend, a classification based on stock exchange listing status
options.C: Shares are classified into preference shares and equity shares; the manner of payment of dividend is dependent upon the nature of shares held
options.D: Shares are classified into 'fully paid-up shares' and 'sweat equity shares' for the purpose of determining the manner of payment of dividend, to the exclusion of the preference/equity distinction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Shares are classified into preference shares and equity shares; the manner of payment of dividend is dependent upon the nature of shares held

For the purpose of dividend payment, shares are classified into two categories: preference shares and equity shares - and, as discussed, the manner of payment of dividend (fixed and preferential versus policy/profit-dependent) is dependent upon which of these two categories a particular share falls into.

question_html: According to section 123(1), from which sources may dividend for any financial year be declared or paid?

options.A: Dividend may be declared or paid only out of the current financial year's profits; profits of previous years, and any money provided by the Government in pursuance of a guarantee, are expressly excluded as sources under section 123(1)
options.B: Dividend may be declared or paid only out of the company's securities premium account, this being the sole source recognised under section 123(1), to the exclusion of current or previous years' profits
options.C: Dividend may be declared or paid out of any reserve of the company, whether or not it qualifies as a 'free reserve' under section 2(43), so long as the reserve appears in the latest audited balance sheet
options.D: (a) Profits of the current financial year, arrived at after providing for depreciation in accordance with Schedule II; (b) profits of any previous financial year or years, similarly arrived at and remaining undistributed (i.e., credit balance in the profit and loss account and free reserves); (c) both (a) and (b); or (d) money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for payment of dividend, in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) (a) Profits of the current financial year, arrived at after providing for depreciation in accordance with Schedule II; (b) profits of any previous financial year or years, similarly arrived at and remaining undistributed (i.e., credit balance in the profit and loss account and free reserves); (c) both (a) and (b); or (d) money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for payment of dividend, in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government

Section 123(1) recognises four sources for declaring/paying dividend: current year's profits (after providing for depreciation as per Schedule II); previous years' undistributed profits (credit balance in profit and loss account and FREE reserves only - per the Third Proviso to section 123(1)); both of these; or money provided by the Central/State Government pursuant to a guarantee given by it.

question_html: Under section 2(43), what does 'free reserves' mean, and what two categories of amount are expressly excluded from this meaning?

options.A: 'Free reserves' means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend; however, (a) any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets (whether shown as a reserve or otherwise), and (b) any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability recognised in equity (including surplus in the profit and loss account on fair-value measurement of the asset/liability), shall NOT be treated as free reserves
options.B: 'Free reserves' means any and every reserve appearing in the latest audited balance sheet of a company, including revaluation reserves and unrealised or notional gains, all of which are freely available for distribution as dividend without restriction
options.C: 'Free reserves' means exclusively the securities premium account and the capital redemption reserve of a company, to the exclusion of any credit balance in the profit and loss account
options.D: 'Free reserves' means reserves created by a company purely for the purpose of expansion or diversification of its business, as distinct from reserves created for any other purpose, this being the sole criterion under section 2(43)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) 'Free reserves' means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend; however, (a) any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets (whether shown as a reserve or otherwise), and (b) any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability recognised in equity (including surplus in the profit and loss account on fair-value measurement of the asset/liability), shall NOT be treated as free reserves

Section 2(43) defines 'free reserves' as reserves which, per the latest audited balance sheet, are available for distribution as dividend - but expressly excludes (a) unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets (however shown), and (b) changes in the carrying amount of an asset/liability recognised in equity (including fair-value-measurement surplus) - precisely because these do not represent real, distributable cash profits.

question_html: Can dividend be declared or paid out of ANY reserve appearing in a company's books, or only out of 'free reserves' as specifically defined?

options.A: Dividend can be declared or paid out of any reserve whatsoever appearing in the company's books, including a capital redemption reserve or a revaluation reserve, without any restriction under the Third Proviso to section 123(1)
options.B: Only free reserves (as defined under section 2(43)) - and no OTHER reserves - are to be used for declaration or payment of dividend, per the Third Proviso to section 123(1)
options.C: Dividend can never be declared or paid out of any reserve under any circumstances; reserves may be used only for issuing bonus shares, and never for declaration or payment of dividend
options.D: Dividend can be declared or paid out of any reserve so long as the Board of Directors, in its own discretion, certifies that reserve to be available for distribution, regardless of whether it meets the statutory definition of 'free reserves'

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Only free reserves (as defined under section 2(43)) - and no OTHER reserves - are to be used for declaration or payment of dividend, per the Third Proviso to section 123(1)

question_html: Why does the law mandate that depreciation be provided for out of profits before dividend can be declared?

options.A: Depreciation must be provided for solely because it is a mandatory requirement under the Income-tax Act, 1961, with no connection at all to the concept of dividend or distributable profits under the Companies Act, 2013
options.B: Depreciation must be provided for only where the company's auditor specifically directs it in the audit report; absent such a specific direction, dividend may validly be declared without any provision for depreciation
options.C: Dividend is an apportionment from revenue profits and should never be declared out of capital; if depreciation is not provided for, the value of the asset and the current year's profits will both be overstated, and declaring dividend out of such overstated profits would, in substance, amount to declaring dividend out of capital - the law therefore mandates provision for depreciation before declaration of dividend
options.D: Depreciation must be provided for only in the case of a company's very first financial year after incorporation; in subsequent years, no such requirement applies before declaration of dividend

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Dividend is an apportionment from revenue profits and should never be declared out of capital; if depreciation is not provided for, the value of the asset and the current year's profits will both be overstated, and declaring dividend out of such overstated profits would, in substance, amount to declaring dividend out of capital - the law therefore mandates provision for depreciation before declaration of dividend

'Depreciation' is a notional estimate of the reduction in an asset's value due to wear and tear, efflux of time, and technological improvements. Without providing for it, the Balance Sheet overstates the asset's value and the current year's profits are similarly overstated - declaring dividend out of such inflated profits would, in effect, be a distribution out of capital (prohibited, as with the prohibition on issuing shares at a discount), leaving inadequate realisable value at winding up even to meet winding-up expenses.

question_html: When computing profits for the purpose of declaring dividend, what must be excluded, per the Proviso to section 123(1)(a)?

options.A: Only losses (and never gains) of any kind are required to be excluded when computing profits for declaration of dividend; all categories of gain, whether realised or unrealised, notional or otherwise, must be fully included
options.B: Only gains arising from the sale of fixed assets in the ordinary course of business are required to be excluded; unrealised or notional gains from mere revaluation of assets (without an actual sale) may validly be included in distributable profits
options.C: Depreciation itself (rather than unrealised/notional/revaluation gains) is the only item required to be excluded when computing profits for declaration of dividend under the Proviso to section 123(1)(a)
options.D: Any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets, and any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability on measurement of the asset/liability at fair value, shall be excluded when computing profits for declaration of dividend

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets, and any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability on measurement of the asset/liability at fair value, shall be excluded when computing profits for declaration of dividend

The Proviso to section 123(1)(a) requires exclusion, in computing profits, of any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains, or revaluation of assets, and any change in the carrying amount of an asset/liability on fair-value measurement - as illustrated by a company that cannot use a revaluation surplus on land (a notional, unrealised gain) towards declaration of dividend, however large the free reserves otherwise available.

question_html: What must be done with carried-over previous losses and depreciation not provided for in previous year(s), before a company declares any dividend for the current year?

options.A: Before declaration of any dividend, carried-over previous losses and depreciation not provided for in the previous year or years are required to be set off against the profit of the company for the current year
options.B: Carried-over previous losses and undepreciated amounts from previous years are simply ignored and have no bearing whatsoever on the computation of current-year profits available for declaration of dividend
options.C: Carried-over previous losses and undepreciated amounts from previous years must be written off exclusively against the company's securities premium account, and never against the current year's profit
options.D: Carried-over previous losses and undepreciated amounts from previous years may, at the Board's discretion, be carried forward indefinitely without ever being set off against any year's profits, even where dividend is proposed to be declared for the current year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Before declaration of any dividend, carried-over previous losses and depreciation not provided for in the previous year or years are required to be set off against the profit of the company for the current year

As a precondition to declaring any dividend, carried-over losses and depreciation not provided for in earlier years must first be set off against the current year's profit - this ensures that dividend is declared only out of genuinely available, current distributable profits, and not out of profits that are illusory once historical shortfalls are accounted for.

question_html: Is a company under any statutory obligation to transfer a specified minimum percentage of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend?

options.A: Yes - every company is statutorily obligated to transfer a minimum of 10% of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend, and cannot declare dividend at all if it fails to do so
options.B: No - transfer of profits to reserves for any financial year has been left entirely to the discretion of the company; a company is free to transfer any portion of its profits to reserves as it may deem fit, and may also decide not to transfer any amount to reserves at all
options.C: Yes - every company is statutorily obligated to transfer a minimum of 5% of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend, this being a fixed floor prescribed under the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014

Correct answer: (B) No - transfer of profits to reserves for any financial year has been left entirely to the discretion of the company; a company is free to transfer any portion of its profits to reserves as it may deem fit, and may also decide not to transfer any amount to reserves at all

Transfer of profits to reserves for any financial year is left to the discretion of the company - it is free to transfer any portion of its profits to reserves as it may deem fit, or to transfer no amount at all, before declaring dividend at whatever rate the Board recommends and the shareholders approve.

question_html: Can a company validly transfer more than 10% of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend at a particular rate, if it considers this appropriate?

options.A: No - a company is statutorily capped at transferring a maximum of 10% of its profits to reserves before declaring dividend, and any transfer in excess of this ceiling is void under the Companies Act, 2013
options.B: No - a company must obtain the prior approval of the National Company Law Tribunal before transferring more than 10% of its profits to reserves in any financial year, regardless of the rate of dividend proposed
options.C: Yes - since the amount to be transferred to reserves out of profits for any financial year, before declaration of dividend, is left entirely to the discretion of the company, it may transfer any part of its profits (including more than 10%) to reserves as it deems fit
options.D: Yes, but only if the company's Articles of Association expressly authorise transfers in excess of 10%; absent such express authorisation, the 10% ceiling applies by default

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - since the amount to be transferred to reserves out of profits for any financial year, before declaration of dividend, is left entirely to the discretion of the company, it may transfer any part of its profits (including more than 10%) to reserves as it deems fit

Because the percentage of profits transferred to reserves before declaration of dividend is left wholly to the company's discretion, there is no statutory ceiling (such as 10%) restricting how much a company may transfer - a company may transfer more than 10% of its profits to reserves if it considers this appropriate, and still validly declare dividend at whatever rate it decides.

question_html: Where a company has no adequate profits in a particular year for declaring dividend, may it still declare dividend, and if so, from what source and subject to what regulatory framework?

options.A: Yes - the company may declare dividend out of the accumulated profits earned by it in previous years and transferred by it to the free reserves, but only in accordance with the procedure laid down in Rule 3 of the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, 2014, and subject to satisfying all of the four conditions prescribed therein

question_html: Under Condition I of Rule 3, at what maximum rate can dividend be declared out of accumulated profits, and in what situation does this condition NOT apply at all?

options.A: The rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the HIGHEST (rather than the average) of the rates at which dividend was declared in the immediately preceding three years, and this condition applies without exception in every case, regardless of the company's dividend history
options.B: The rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared by the company in the immediately preceding three years [Rate of Dividend ≤ (RD1+RD2+RD3)/3]; however, this condition shall not apply at all if the company has not declared any dividend in each of the three preceding financial years
options.C: The rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared in the immediately preceding FIVE (rather than three) years, and this condition has no exception under any circumstances
options.D: The rate of dividend declared shall not exceed 10% flat, regardless of the company's dividend history in the immediately preceding three years, this being the correct content of Condition I under Rule 3

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The rate of dividend declared shall not exceed the average of the rates at which dividend was declared by the company in the immediately preceding three years [Rate of Dividend ≤ (RD1+RD2+RD3)/3]; however, this condition shall not apply at all if the company has not declared any dividend in each of the three preceding financial years

question_html: Under Condition II of Rule 3, what is the ceiling on the total amount that may be drawn from accumulated profits for declaration of dividend?

options.A: The total amount to be drawn from such accumulated profits shall not exceed 25% of its paid-up share capital alone, with free reserves being wholly excluded from this ceiling computation under Condition II
options.B: The total amount to be drawn from such accumulated profits shall not exceed a flat sum of rupees fifty lakh, irrespective of the size of the company's paid-up share capital or free reserves
options.C: The total amount to be drawn from such accumulated profits shall not exceed 10% of its paid-up share capital and free reserves as appearing in the latest audited financial statement

question_html: Under Condition III of Rule 3, in what order must the amount drawn from accumulated profits be applied, where the company has incurred a loss in the current financial year in which dividend is declared?

options.A: The amount so drawn may be applied directly towards declaration of dividend on equity shares first, with any residual balance thereafter being utilised, at the company's discretion, to set off the current year's losses
options.B: Condition III has no bearing on the order of application at all; the amount drawn may be freely apportioned between loss set-off and dividend declaration in whatever proportion the Board of Directors considers fit

answer_html:

question_html: Under Condition IV of Rule 3, what floor must the balance of free reserves satisfy immediately after the withdrawal for declaration of dividend?

options.A: The balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below 15% of its paid-up share capital as appearing in the latest audited financial statement [i.e., Free Reserves - Amount of withdrawal ≥ 15% of paid-up share capital]
options.B: The balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below 50% of its paid-up share capital as appearing in the latest audited financial statement, this being the correct floor prescribed under Condition IV of Rule 3
options.C: Condition IV imposes no floor at all on the balance of reserves remaining after withdrawal; the entirety of the free reserves may validly be exhausted in declaring dividend out of accumulated profits
options.D: The balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below 15% of the company's total paid-up share capital AND free reserves combined (rather than paid-up share capital alone), as appearing in the latest audited financial statement

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The balance of reserves after such withdrawal shall not fall below 15% of its paid-up share capital as appearing in the latest audited financial statement [i.e., Free Reserves - Amount of withdrawal ≥ 15% of paid-up share capital]

Condition IV requires that, after withdrawing the amount used for set-off of losses and declaration of dividend, the balance of free reserves must not fall below 15% of the company's paid-up share capital as per the latest audited financial statement - a floor designed to preserve a minimum cushion of reserves. All four conditions under Rule 3 must be satisfied simultaneously.

question_html: Are the conditions prescribed under Rule 3 (governing declaration of dividend out of accumulated profits) applicable to every Government company?

options.A: Yes - the conditions prescribed by Rule 3 apply, without any exemption whatsoever, to every Government company, in exactly the same manner as they apply to any other class of company under the Companies Act, 2013
options.B: No - the conditions prescribed by Rule 3 are not applicable to a Government company in which the entire paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, or by any State Government or Governments, or by the Central Government and one or more State Governments (per Notification No. 463(E), dated 05-06-2015)

question_html: Under section 123(5), to whom is dividend payable, and can a purchaser of shares whose name has not yet been entered in the Register of Members claim payment of dividend to himself?

options.A: Dividend shall be payable to whoever is in physical possession of the share certificate at the time of payment, regardless of whether that person's name appears in the Register of Members as the registered shareholder
options.B: A purchaser of shares whose name has not yet been entered in the Register of Members can always claim payment of dividend directly to himself, so long as he can prove he has made full payment of the purchase price to the seller of the shares
options.C: Dividend is payable exclusively to the company's own bankers for onward remittance, and can never be paid directly to the registered shareholder, his order, or his own banker
options.D: Dividend shall be payable only to the registered shareholder of such share, or to his order, or to his banker; a purchaser of shares whose name is NOT entered in the Register of Members cannot claim payment of dividend to himself, even though he might have made full payment to the seller of the shares

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Dividend shall be payable only to the registered shareholder of such share, or to his order, or to his banker; a purchaser of shares whose name is NOT entered in the Register of Members cannot claim payment of dividend to himself, even though he might have made full payment to the seller of the shares

Section 123(5) confines payment of dividend to the registered shareholder of the share, or to his order, or to his banker (and if the company pays a banker so nominated, this is deemed payment to the shareholder himself) - a purchaser not yet entered in the Register of Members cannot claim dividend to himself merely because he has paid the seller in full; section 126 separately governs keeping dividend in abeyance pending registration of a share transfer.

question_html: What is the 'record date' announced by a company for the purpose of dividend, and who is entitled to the dividend based on it?

options.A: The record date is the date announced by the company for determining entitlement to dividend; all persons whose names are included in the Register of Members on that date shall be entitled to dividend, regardless of when they acquired their shares relative to the AGM at which the dividend was approved
options.B: The 'record date' refers exclusively to the date on which the Annual General Meeting approving the dividend is actually held, and has no independent significance apart from that meeting date
options.C: Entitlement to dividend is determined not by the record date at all, but solely by who held the shares on the first day of the relevant financial year, twelve months or more before the AGM
options.D: The 'record date' is a date fixed unilaterally by the Registrar of Companies (rather than announced by the company itself) for determining entitlement to dividend

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The record date is the date announced by the company for determining entitlement to dividend; all persons whose names are included in the Register of Members on that date shall be entitled to dividend, regardless of when they acquired their shares relative to the AGM at which the dividend was approved

The record date is the date announced by the company for determining entitlement to dividend - all persons whose names appear in the Register of Members on that date are entitled to the dividend. Thus, where a shareholder transfers shares and the transferee's name is entered in the register on or before the record date, the transferee (not the original transferor) is entitled to the dividend, even if the transferor held the shares for a much longer period historically.

question_html: In what modes may dividend be paid, given that dividends are payable in cash and not in kind, and what is the recognised exception to the 'cash only' rule?

options.A: Dividend may be paid in cash, in kind (such as by transfer of the company's own products or inventory), or by allotment of further equity shares of the company, all being equally permissible modes of payment under section 123(5)
options.B: Dividends payable to shareholders in cash may be paid by cheque, dividend warrant, or through any electronic mode; the exception to the 'cash only' rule is the capitalisation of profits/reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares, or for paying up any amount unpaid on shares held by members - though such bonus shares cannot be issued IN LIEU of dividend
options.C: Dividends are payable exclusively by physical cash handed over in person to the registered shareholder; payment by cheque, dividend warrant, or electronic mode is not recognised as a valid mode of payment of dividend at all
options.D: There is no exception at all to the 'cash only' rule for payment of dividend; capitalisation of profits/reserves for issuing bonus shares is treated, in every case, as a mode of paying dividend in kind

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Dividends payable to shareholders in cash may be paid by cheque, dividend warrant, or through any electronic mode; the exception to the 'cash only' rule is the capitalisation of profits/reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares, or for paying up any amount unpaid on shares held by members - though such bonus shares cannot be issued IN LIEU of dividend

Dividends are payable only in cash (cheque, dividend warrant, or electronic mode being recognised cash-payment channels) - the First Proviso to section 123(5) carves out an exception only for capitalisation of profits/reserves to issue fully paid-up bonus shares, or to pay up unpaid amounts on shares held by members; however, declaration of dividend does not affect the power to issue bonus shares, but such shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend.

question_html: What modification applies to section 123(5) in its application to Nidhi companies, per Notification No. GSR 465(E), dated 05-06-2015?

options.A: Nidhis are wholly exempted from the requirement to pay dividend in cash, and may instead pay dividend entirely in kind, by transfer of gold or other commodities to their members
options.B: Nidhis are required to pay dividend exclusively by dividend warrant sent by registered post, to the exclusion of payment by cheque, electronic mode, or crediting to the member's account under any circumstances
options.C: In the case of Nidhis, any dividend payable in cash may be paid by crediting the same to the account of the member, if the dividend is not claimed within 30 days from the date of declaration of the dividend
options.D: Nidhis are permitted to defer payment of dividend indefinitely, without any obligation to credit the amount to the member's account even where the dividend remains unclaimed beyond 30 days from declaration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) In the case of Nidhis, any dividend payable in cash may be paid by crediting the same to the account of the member, if the dividend is not claimed within 30 days from the date of declaration of the dividend

Per Notification No. GSR 465(E), dated 05-06-2015, section 123(5) applies to Nidhis subject to the modification that any dividend payable in cash may be paid by crediting it to the member's account, specifically where the dividend is not claimed within 30 days from the date of its declaration.

question_html: Under section 123(6), can a company that has failed to comply with the provisions of sections 73 (prohibition on acceptance of deposits from the public) and 74 (repayment of deposits accepted before commencement of the 2013 Act) declare any dividend on its equity shares?

options.A: Yes - a company failing to comply with sections 73 and 74 may nonetheless freely declare dividend on its equity shares, so long as it separately discloses the ongoing default in the notes to its financial statements
options.B: No - such a company is permanently and irretrievably barred from ever declaring dividend on its equity shares in the future, even after the default under sections 73/74 is fully rectified
options.C: Yes, but only up to a maximum rate of 5%, this being the statutory ceiling applicable to a company in default of sections 73 and 74 under section 123(6)
options.D: No - a company which fails to comply with the provisions of sections 73 and 74 shall NOT, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - a company which fails to comply with the provisions of sections 73 and 74 shall NOT, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares

Section 123(6) prohibits a company that fails to comply with sections 73 (prohibition on acceptance of deposits from the public) and 74 (repayment of pre-2013-Act deposits) from declaring any dividend on its equity shares, so long as such failure CONTINUES - the prohibition is tied to the continuation of the default, and lifts once the default is cured (not permanent).

question_html: Where a dividend has been declared by a company but has not been paid or claimed within 30 days from the date of declaration, what must the company do, and within what further time limit?

options.A: The company shall, within seven (7) days from the expiry of the said period of 30 days, transfer the total amount of unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account, called the Unpaid Dividend Account (UDA), opened by the company in any scheduled bank
options.B: The company must permanently forfeit the unpaid or unclaimed dividend amount to its own general reserve, with no obligation to open or transfer such amount to any separate Unpaid Dividend Account at all
options.C: The company must, within 90 days (rather than 7 days) from expiry of the 30-day non-payment period, transfer the total amount of unpaid or unclaimed dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account
options.D: The company must transfer the unpaid or unclaimed dividend amount directly to the Investor Education and Protection Fund within 7 days of the expiry of the 30-day period, bypassing the Unpaid Dividend Account entirely

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The company shall, within seven (7) days from the expiry of the said period of 30 days, transfer the total amount of unpaid or unclaimed dividend to a special account, called the Unpaid Dividend Account (UDA), opened by the company in any scheduled bank

Section 124(1) requires that where dividend declared has not been paid or claimed within 30 days of declaration, the company shall, within 7 days from expiry of that 30-day period, transfer the total unpaid/unclaimed amount to a special Unpaid Dividend Account (UDA) opened by it in any scheduled bank.

question_html: Within what time of transferring amounts to the Unpaid Dividend Account must the company prepare and publish a statement of the unpaid dividend, and what must this statement, and its manner of publication, contain?

options.A: The company has no obligation at all to prepare or publish any statement of unpaid dividend; the Unpaid Dividend Account, once opened, requires no further disclosure of the names or amounts involved
options.B: Within 90 days of transferring any amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account, the company shall prepare a statement containing the names, last known addresses, and the amount of unpaid dividend to be paid to each person, and place such statement on its website (if any) and also on any other website approved by the Central Government for this purpose
options.C: The company must prepare and publish the statement within 30 days (rather than 90 days) of transferring the amount, and the statement need only be filed with the Registrar, without any requirement of publication on the company's or any Government-approved website
options.D: The statement need only record the AGGREGATE amount of unpaid dividend transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account, without any requirement to disclose individual shareholders' names, addresses, or amounts

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Within 90 days of transferring any amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account, the company shall prepare a statement containing the names, last known addresses, and the amount of unpaid dividend to be paid to each person, and place such statement on its website (if any) and also on any other website approved by the Central Government for this purpose

question_html: If a company defaults in transferring the total unpaid dividend amount (or any part thereof) to the Unpaid Dividend Account, what is the consequence, and who benefits from it?

options.A: The company shall pay interest at the rate of 18% per annum (rather than 12% per annum) on the amount not transferred, with such interest accruing to the benefit of the Central Government rather than the members
options.B: There is no interest consequence at all for a company's default in transferring the unpaid dividend amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account; the only consequence is a discretionary penalty imposed by the Registrar
options.C: The company shall pay, from the date of such default, interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the amount not so transferred to the UDA; the interest accruing on such amount shall enure (i.e., be available) to the benefit of the members of the company in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them
options.D: The interest payable for default in transferring the amount enures to the benefit of the company's statutory auditor (as a form of compensation for reporting the default), rather than to the members whose dividend remains unpaid

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The company shall pay, from the date of such default, interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the amount not so transferred to the UDA; the interest accruing on such amount shall enure (i.e., be available) to the benefit of the members of the company in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them

Section 124(3) fixes the consequence of default in transferring the unpaid dividend amount to the UDA at interest of 12% per annum, running from the date of default, on the amount not so transferred - and this interest is expressly stated to enure to the benefit of the members, in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them (not to the company or any third party).

question_html: Where money transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account remains unpaid or unclaimed for seven (7) years from the date of transfer, what must the company do with (a) the money, and (b) the underlying shares in respect of which such dividend was not paid or claimed?

question_html: Can the original owner of shares transferred to the IEPF reclaim them, and does the transfer of shares to the IEPF still occur if dividend was paid or claimed for even one year during the relevant 7 consecutive years?

options.A: Yes - any claimant of shares transferred to the IEPF is entitled to reclaim the 'transferred shares' from the IEPF, in accordance with the prescribed procedure and on submission of prescribed documents; and by way of Explanation, if any dividend is paid or claimed for ANY year during the said period of 7 consecutive years, the shares shall NOT be transferred to the IEPF
options.B: No - once shares are transferred to the IEPF, the original owner permanently and irretrievably loses all rights to reclaim them under any circumstances, regardless of the prescribed procedure or documentation submitted
options.C: Yes, a claimant may reclaim transferred shares, but the transfer of shares to the IEPF still occurs even if dividend was paid or claimed for every one of the 7 consecutive years, since the Explanation to section 124(6) has no bearing on this outcome
options.D: No - the right to reclaim shares from the IEPF is available only to the company itself (and never to the original shareholder or claimant), rendering the shareholder's own right of reclaim illusory

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - any claimant of shares transferred to the IEPF is entitled to reclaim the 'transferred shares' from the IEPF, in accordance with the prescribed procedure and on submission of prescribed documents; and by way of Explanation, if any dividend is paid or claimed for ANY year during the said period of 7 consecutive years, the shares shall NOT be transferred to the IEPF

question_html: Where a company fails to pay a declared dividend, or fails to post the dividend warrant, within 30 days of declaration, what punishment is prescribed, and what is one recognised exemption from such punishment?

options.A: The only consequence prescribed under section 127 is a flat monetary penalty on the company of Rs. 1 lakh, with no imprisonment for directors and no exemptions of any kind recognised under the section

case_facts_html: Whitmore Textiles Limited had declared final dividend at the rate of 9% in FY 2023-24, 11% in FY 2024-25, and 13% in FY 2025-26. During FY 2026-27, the company incurred a loss for the period up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date on which the Board proposes to declare an interim dividend. Notwithstanding this loss, the Board of Directors wishes to declare an interim dividend at the rate of 13%, considering that the company had declared dividend at that very rate in the immediately preceding financial year.
question_html:
Whitmore Textiles Limited had declared final dividend at the rate of 9% in FY 2023-24, 11% in FY 2024-25, and 13% in FY 2025-26. During FY 2026-27, the company incurred a loss for the period up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date on which the Board proposes to declare an interim dividend. Notwithstanding this loss, the Board of Directors wishes to declare an interim dividend at the rate of 13%, considering that the company had declared dividend at that very rate in the immediately preceding financial year.

What is the maximum rate at which Whitmore Textiles Limited's Board of Directors can validly declare interim dividend for FY 2026-27, given the loss incurred up to the end of the preceding quarter?

options.A: 13% - since the company had declared dividend at exactly this rate in the immediately preceding financial year (2025-26), the Board is entitled to declare interim dividend at that same rate despite the current-year loss
options.B: 13% - the average-rate cap under the proviso to section 123(3) applies only to final dividend, and has no application at all to interim dividend, so the Board may validly declare interim dividend at any rate it considers fit
options.C: 11% - since the company has incurred a loss up to the end of the quarter preceding the date of declaration, the proviso to section 123(3) caps the interim dividend rate at the average of the rates declared in the immediately preceding three financial years, i.e., (9% + 11% + 13%) / 3 = 11%; the Board's proposal to declare interim dividend at 13% is therefore not valid
options.D: 9% - the proviso to section 123(3) caps interim dividend, in a loss year, at the LOWEST (rather than the average) of the rates declared in the immediately preceding three financial years

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 11% - since the company has incurred a loss up to the end of the quarter preceding the date of declaration, the proviso to section 123(3) caps the interim dividend rate at the average of the rates declared in the immediately preceding three financial years, i.e., (9% + 11% + 13%) / 3 = 11%; the Board's proposal to declare interim dividend at 13% is therefore not valid

The proviso to section 123(3) caps interim dividend, where a loss has been incurred up to the end of the preceding quarter, at the average of the rates declared in the immediately preceding three financial years: (9+11+13)/3 = 11%. The Board's proposal to declare interim dividend at 13% - merely because that was last year's rate - is not valid; the correct benchmark is the three-year average, not the most recent year's rate alone.

Suppose, hypothetically, Whitmore Textiles Limited had NOT incurred any loss during FY 2026-27 up to the end of the quarter preceding the proposed date of declaration. Would the Board then be bound by the 11% average-rate cap in declaring interim dividend for that year?

options.A: No - the average-rate cap under the proviso to section 123(3) applies only where the company has incurred a loss during the current financial year up to the end of the quarter immediately preceding the date of declaration of interim dividend; absent such a loss, this specific averaging constraint does not apply, and the Board may recommend a rate based on the sources permitted under section 123(3) without being bound by the three-year average

Nightingale Pharma Limited, at its Annual General Meeting held on 5th September, 2026, declared a final dividend of Rs. 4 per equity share of face value Rs. 10 each, and announced 12th September, 2026, as the record date for determining entitlement to dividend. Mr. Rakesh, who held 3,000 equity shares of Nightingale Pharma since 2022, transferred all his shares to Ms. Divya in August 2026. The instrument of transfer was duly lodged with the company, and Ms. Divya's name was entered in the Register of Members on 10th September, 2026 - i.e., before the record date. Separately, Nightingale Pharma's Articles of Association authorise the company, under section 51, to pay dividend in proportion to the amount paid up on each share; certain other equity shareholders hold shares of face value Rs. 10 each on which only Rs. 6 has been paid up.

As between Mr. Rakesh (the original, long-standing holder) and Ms. Divya (the transferee whose name was entered in the Register of Members before the record date), who is entitled to receive the dividend declared by Nightingale Pharma Limited?

options.A: Ms. Divya is entitled to the dividend - since her name was entered in the Register of Members on 10th September, 2026, which is before the record date of 12th September, 2026, she is the registered shareholder on the record date, and dividend is payable to the person whose name appears in the Register of Members on the record date, regardless of how long the original holder (Mr. Rakesh) had held the shares in the past
options.B: Mr. Rakesh is entitled to the dividend, since he held the shares for a much longer period (since 2022) than Ms. Divya, and length of prior holding - rather than registration on the record date - is the determinative factor under section 123(5)
options.C: Neither Mr. Rakesh nor Ms. Divya is entitled to the dividend, since a share transfer occurring at any point during the same financial year as the AGM automatically disqualifies both the transferor and the transferee from receiving that year's dividend
options.D: Both Mr. Rakesh and Ms. Divya are entitled to receive the dividend in equal proportion, this 50:50 split being the default statutory rule wherever a share transfer occurs between the end of the financial year and the record date

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Ms. Divya is entitled to the dividend - since her name was entered in the Register of Members on 10th September, 2026, which is before the record date of 12th September, 2026, she is the registered shareholder on the record date, and dividend is payable to the person whose name appears in the Register of Members on the record date, regardless of how long the original holder (Mr. Rakesh) had held the shares in the past

Dividend is paid to the person whose name is entered in the Register of Members on the record date announced by the company. Since Ms. Divya's name was entered on 10th September, 2026 - before the record date of 12th September, 2026 - she is the registered shareholder on the record date, and is accordingly entitled to the dividend, regardless of Mr. Rakesh's much longer historical holding period.

Suppose, in a variant of these facts, a different purchaser had lodged his transfer instrument with Nightingale Pharma, but the transfer had NOT been registered (i.e., his name was not entered in the Register of Members) by the record date. Could such a purchaser claim payment of dividend directly to himself?

options.A: Yes - any purchaser who has lodged a transfer instrument with the company (regardless of whether the transfer has actually been registered by the record date) is automatically entitled to claim dividend directly to himself under section 123(5)
options.B: No - a purchaser of shares whose name is not entered in the Register of Members cannot claim payment of dividend to himself, even though he might have made full payment to the seller; under section 126, the company must transfer the dividend relating to such shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account, unless the REGISTERED holder has authorised the company in writing to pay such dividend to the transferee
options.C: No - such a purchaser permanently forfeits all rights to the dividend for that year, and section 126 provides no mechanism at all by which the registered holder could authorise payment to him instead
options.D: Yes, but only if the purchaser is able to produce the original share certificate as proof of purchase, this documentary proof alone being sufficient to override the Register of Members for purposes of dividend entitlement

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - a purchaser of shares whose name is not entered in the Register of Members cannot claim payment of dividend to himself, even though he might have made full payment to the seller; under section 126, the company must transfer the dividend relating to such shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account, unless the REGISTERED holder has authorised the company in writing to pay such dividend to the transferee

Section 123(5) confines payment of dividend to the registered shareholder - a purchaser whose transfer is not yet registered cannot claim dividend to himself merely on the strength of having paid the seller. Section 126 additionally requires the company to transfer such dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account, UNLESS the registered holder has authorised, in writing, payment of the dividend to the transferee named in the transfer instrument.

Separately, Nightingale Pharma's Articles of Association authorise the company, under section 51, to pay dividend in proportion to the amount paid up on each share; certain other equity shareholders hold shares of face value Rs. 10 each on which only Rs. 6 has been paid up.

For the equity shareholders of Nightingale Pharma Limited holding partly-paid shares (face value Rs. 10, of which only Rs. 6 has been paid up), and given the company's Articles authorise payment of dividend in proportion to the amount paid up (per section 51), what amount of dividend per share is such a partly-paid shareholder entitled to receive, out of the declared dividend of Rs. 4 per fully-paid share?

options.A: Rs. 4.00 per share - since dividend is declared at a flat rate of Rs. 4 per equity share regardless of the amount paid up, partly-paid shareholders are entitled to exactly the same amount per share as fully-paid shareholders, irrespective of what the Articles provide under section 51
options.B: Nil - a company is absolutely prohibited under section 51 from paying any dividend at all to holders of partly-paid shares, even where the Articles specifically authorise proportionate payment based on the amount paid up
options.C: Rs. 2.40 per share - since the Articles authorise proportionate payment under section 51, and only Rs. 6 out of the Rs. 10 face value has been paid up, the dividend payable is Rs. 4 x (6/10) = Rs. 2.40 per partly-paid share, rather than the full Rs. 4 per share paid to fully-paid shareholders
options.D: Rs. 6.00 per share - the dividend payable to a partly-paid shareholder is computed as the AMOUNT PAID UP per share (Rs. 6), rather than as a proportion applied to the declared dividend rate of Rs. 4 per share

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 2.40 per share - since the Articles authorise proportionate payment under section 51, and only Rs. 6 out of the Rs. 10 face value has been paid up, the dividend payable is Rs. 4 x (6/10) = Rs. 2.40 per partly-paid share, rather than the full Rs. 4 per share paid to fully-paid shareholders

Section 51 permits a company, if authorised by its Articles, to pay dividend in proportion to the amount paid up on each share. Since Nightingale Pharma's Articles so authorise, and the shares in question are paid up to the extent of Rs. 6 out of Rs. 10 face value, the proportionate dividend is Rs. 4 x (6/10) = Rs. 2.40 per share, rather than the full Rs. 4 per share payable on fully-paid equity shares.

Suppose, instead, Ashgrove Constructions had been incorporated as a company licensed under section 8 (formed with charitable objects). Would curing any default (in the manner discussed above) enable such a Section 8 company to declare dividend to its members?

options.A: Yes - a Section 8 company is subject to exactly the same default-contingent prohibition under section 123(6) as any other company, and curing the default (e.g., under section 74) would equally enable it to declare dividend to its members
options.B: No - unlike the section 123(6) prohibition (which is default-contingent and lifts once the default is cured), a company licensed under section 8 is prohibited from paying ANY dividend to its members at all, absolutely and without exception, since its profits are intended to be applied only in promoting the objects for which it was formed - curing an unrelated default would not change this position
options.C: Yes - a Section 8 company is entitled to declare dividend freely at any time, since section 8(1) applies only to for-profit companies and has no application at all to a company formed with charitable objects
options.D: No, but only until the Section 8 company's licence is renewed for a further period; upon renewal of the licence, the absolute prohibition on paying dividend converts into the ordinary, default-contingent prohibition under section 123(6)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - unlike the section 123(6) prohibition (which is default-contingent and lifts once the default is cured), a company licensed under section 8 is prohibited from paying ANY dividend to its members at all, absolutely and without exception, since its profits are intended to be applied only in promoting the objects for which it was formed - curing an unrelated default would not change this position

Section 8(1) imposes an ABSOLUTE prohibition on a company licensed under that section from paying any dividend to its members - because its profits must be applied only towards promoting its charitable objects - unlike the section 123(6) prohibition (applicable to ordinary defaulting companies), which is contingent on, and lifts upon curing, the underlying default. Curing an unrelated default (such as one under section 74) would have no bearing on a Section 8 company's absolute inability to pay dividend to its members.

Coralridge Foods Limited declared a final dividend at its AGM held on 1st August, 2026. A portion of the dividend, amounting to Rs. 8,00,000, remained unpaid/unclaimed even after 30 days from the date of declaration. Separately, dividend amounting to Rs. 1,50,000, relating to certain other shares of Coralridge Foods, has remained continuously unpaid and unclaimed by the concerned shareholders for a full 7 consecutive years since being transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account, with no dividend having been paid or claimed in respect of those shares during that entire 7-year period.

Is Coralridge Foods Limited liable to pay interest on the Rs. 8,00,000 amount, given its 22-day delay (beyond the 7-day window) in transferring the amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account, and if so, at what rate and for whose benefit?

options.A: No - section 124(3) imposes interest liability only where the company fails to transfer the amount to the UDA at all (i.e., permanently), and a mere 22-day delay in transfer (where the transfer is eventually made) attracts no interest liability whatsoever
options.B: Yes, but at the rate of 18% per annum (rather than 12% per annum) since 18% is the general default rate of interest applicable under the Companies Act, 2013 wherever a company fails to meet a prescribed statutory timeline
options.C: Yes - under section 124(3), since Coralridge Foods defaulted in transferring the amount to the UDA within the prescribed 7-day window, it is liable to pay interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the Rs. 8,00,000, running from the date of such default (i.e., from the date the 7-day window expired) until the amount is actually transferred; this interest enures to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them
options.D: Yes, but the resulting interest liability enures to the benefit of the Central Government (via the Consolidated Fund of India) rather than to the members whose dividend remained unpaid

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - under section 124(3), since Coralridge Foods defaulted in transferring the amount to the UDA within the prescribed 7-day window, it is liable to pay interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the Rs. 8,00,000, running from the date of such default (i.e., from the date the 7-day window expired) until the amount is actually transferred; this interest enures to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them

Section 124(3) fixes 12% p.a. interest, running from the date of default, on any amount not transferred to the UDA within the prescribed 7-day window - Coralridge Foods' 22-day delay squarely attracts this liability on the Rs. 8,00,000, and the resulting interest enures to the benefit of the members in proportion to the amount remaining unpaid to them (not to the company or the Government).
